hints: Focus on what actually reacts, since only the pure MCO3 part of the 7.4 g sample produces the chloride.
Work out the mass of pure MCO3 first, 57% of 7.4 g is 4.218 g, and remember this must give 0.050 mol of product.
Use moles equals mass divided by Mr to find Mr of MCO3, then subtract 60 for CO3 to leave the metal's atomic mass.
walkthrough:
**Find the mass of pure carbonate**

Only part of X is useful. The rest is unreactive impurity, so start by finding the real reacting mass.

$$\text{mass of MCO}_3 = \frac{57}{100} \times 7.4 = 4.218 \text{ g}$$

**Link moles of carbonate to moles of chloride**

Write the equation to check the mole ratio. It is a simple 1 to 1 link.

$$\text{MCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MCl}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So moles of $\text{MCO}_3$ reacted = moles of $\text{MCl}_2$ made = $0.050 \text{ mol}$.

**Calculate Mr and identify M**

Now use moles and mass to find the molar mass of the carbonate, then take away the carbonate group.

$$M_r(\text{MCO}_3) = \frac{4.218}{0.050} = 84.36$$
$$A_r(\text{M}) = 84.36 - 60.0 = 24.36$$
This is very close to 24.3, so M is magnesium.

options.A: Correct. Mr of MCO3 is about 84.4, giving Ar of M about 24.4. This matches Mg (Ar = 24.3). The 1:1 mole ratio makes this deduction secure.
options.B: Incorrect. Ca has Ar 40.1, so CaCO3 would have Mr 100.1. 0.050 mol would need 5.0 g of pure CaCO3, much more than the 4.218 g present. This trap comes from forgetting to correct for the 57% purity.
options.C: Incorrect. Sr has Ar 87.6, so SrCO3 has Mr about 147.6. 0.050 mol would need about 7.38 g of pure carbonate, almost the whole impure sample. It ignores the impurity calculation.
options.D: Incorrect. Ba has Ar 137.3, so BaCO3 has Mr about 197.3. 0.050 mol would need about 9.87 g, which is even more than the total 7.4 g sample. Impossible here.
